items.prose: Fifteen coins lie heads up. A move turns over exactly six of them.
items.question: Can moves ever leave all fifteen tails up?

options.text: Yes: 15 is not a multiple of 6, but tails can be turned back
options.why: Turning tails back changes the heads by an even amount too: $6 - 2k$. The heads stay odd.
Three moves turn 18 coins, but the heads change by an even number each time, and 15 is odd.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find how one move changes the number of heads.

byKey.yes: A move turning $k$ heads changes the heads by $6 - 2k$, an even number, so they stay odd.
byKey.three: Each move changes the heads by an even number, so 15 heads never reach 0.

explain.text: A move turning $k$ heads and $6 - k$ tails changes the heads by $6 - 2k$, an even number. So the heads stay odd, and all tails needs 0. Principle: parity is the first invariant to try.

items.prose: A 7 × 7 board loses its centre square.
items.question: Can 24 dominoes cover the other 48 squares?

options.text: No: an odd board cannot be tiled
options.why: The board is no longer odd: 48 squares remain, 24 dark and 24 light.

options.text: Only if a corner is removed instead
options.why: The centre is dark too, like the corners, so the colours balance.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the colours left, then look for a tiling.

byKey.no: 48 squares remain, and the colours balance at 24 and 24.
byKey.corner: The centre has the corners' colour, so removing it balances the board as well.

explain.text: The centre is dark, so 24 dark and 24 light squares remain. Balance only allows a tiling, but here one exists: rings of dominoes round the hole, which a search confirms. Principle: after the count allows it, build the tiling.

items.prose: A drawer holds ten pairs of gloves, five black pairs and five brown, all loose. You draw in the dark.
items.question: How many gloves must you take to be sure of a wearable pair: one colour, one left and one right?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Build the worst case: what can you hold with no wearable pair?

byKey.three: Three gloves give two of one colour, but they may both be left gloves.
byKey.five: Five gloves can all be left gloves.
byKey.twentyone: There are only 20 gloves. The worst case is all ten left gloves.

explain.text: The worst case holds all ten left gloves: no wearable pair. The eleventh is a right glove, and it matches a left glove of its colour. Principle: the worst case is the biggest collection with no success.

items.prose: A hundred coins, one heavier, and a balance.
items.question: What is the fewest weighings that always finds the heavy coin?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare 100 with the powers of 3.

byKey.four: Four weighings handle $3^4 = 81$ coins, fewer than 100.

explain.text: Four weighings give 81 outcomes, too few for 100 coins; five give 243. Split 100 as 34, 33 and 33, and keep splitting into thirds. Principle: the smallest $k$ with $3^k \ge n$.

items.prose: A 6-minute and an 11-minute hourglass. You may turn either over whenever one of them empties.
items.question: Order the steps that measure 16 minutes. One line does not belong.

lines.text: At 6 minutes the 6 empties; turn it over.
At 11 minutes the 11 empties; the 6 has run 5 minutes since its turn.
Turn the 6 over: its 5 minutes of sand run back.
At 11 minutes, turn the 6 over and let it run a full 6 minutes.
lines.why: That ends at 17. The 6 holds only 5 minutes of run sand at 11.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each turn waits for a glass to empty.

byKey.d1: At 11 the 6 has only 5 minutes below, so turning it runs 5, not 6.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the full 6 minutes belongs.

explain.text: Start both and turn the 6 when it empties. At 11 the 6 has 5 minutes of sand below, and turning it runs those back: 16. Principle: a glass turned mid-run stores the time it has run.

items.prose: A 4 × 4 grid of lamps starts all off. A move toggles every lamp in one row or one column.
items.question: Which numbers of lit lamps can you reach? Select all that apply.

options.why: Toggling $r$ rows and $c$ columns lights $4r + 4c - 2rc$ lamps, and no choice gives 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the lit lamps after toggling $r$ rows and $c$ columns.

explain.text: Toggling $r$ rows and $c$ columns lights $r(4 - c) + c(4 - r) = 4r + 4c - 2rc$ lamps. With $r$ and $c$ from 0 to 4 that gives 0, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 16. All 128 reachable patterns have these counts.

items.prose: A 4 × 7 board has 28 squares, 14 dark and 14 light. Seven T-tetrominoes have 28 squares too.
items.question: Can seven T-tetrominoes cover the board?

options.text: Yes: the area and the colours both balance
options.why: Each T covers 3 of one shade and 1 of the other. Seven of them cannot balance 14 and 14.

options.text: Yes, if the pieces may be turned over
options.why: Turning a T over does not change its colour split of 3 and 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Track dark minus light, one T at a time.

byKey.yes: Each T adds ±2 to dark minus light, and seven such terms cannot sum to 0.
byKey.rotate: Every placement of a T still covers 3 of one shade and 1 of the other.

explain.text: On a chessboard each T covers 3 of one shade and 1 of the other: ±2 to dark minus light. Seven terms of ±2 sum to an odd multiple of 2, never 0, but the board needs 0. A search of every placement agrees.

items.prose: You pick numbers from 1 to 100, as unluckily as you like.
items.question: How many must you pick to be sure that two of them are consecutive?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pair the numbers into boxes of two consecutive numbers.

byKey.fifty: Fifty can fail: the 50 odd numbers contain no consecutive pair.
byKey.hundred: Far fewer suffice: pair 1 with 2, 3 with 4, and so on.
byKey.two: Two numbers are consecutive only by luck.

explain.text: Pairs 1 and 2, 3 and 4, up to 99 and 100 make fifty boxes. So 51 picks force a pair, and the 50 odd numbers show 50 can fail. Principle: boxes of two that always work, then one more than the boxes.

items.prose: Ten bags of coins. Genuine coins weigh 10 g; one bag holds only fakes of 9 g. You take $k$ coins from bag $k$ and weigh them all once. The scale reads 542 g.
items.question: Which bag holds the fakes?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the reading with the all-genuine weight.

byKey.fiftyfive: 55 is the number of coins taken. The shortfall names the bag.
byKey.two: 542 is 2 above 540, but compare with 550, the all-genuine weight.

explain.text: The 55 coins would weigh 550 g if all were genuine. Each fake is 1 g light, so 8 g short means eight fakes: bag 8. Principle: one reading can name a suspect when each suspect leaves its own signature.
